title: Grand County Colorado well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Grand County, Colorado, median well depth is about 190 ft, with most yields between 6–11.5 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and reliability.
h1: Understanding wells in Grand County, Colorado
intro_html:
Grand County wells are classic mountain-bedrock wells: variable depth, but generally decent production. The state has records on 11,182 permits here, so we have a pretty good picture of what you’re likely to hit in places like Granby, Fraser, Kremmling, and Grand Lake.

I’ll walk through how deep wells usually go, how much water they make, what the water table is doing, who’s been drilling, what a new well is likely to cost, and the main risks to look for before you buy or build.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Grand County
sections.html:
Across Grand County, the median well depth is about 190 feet, but there’s a wide spread. The middle half of wells land between 100 and 325 feet, and about 25% are under 100 feet. Another 25% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and roughly 7% go past 600 feet. The deepest well on record goes down 2,125 feet.

For a driller’s bid, that 100–325 foot “middle band” is the realistic planning range for most home sites in the fractured-bedrock aquifer that underlies nearly all 11,013 recorded bedrock wells. Outliers toward 500 feet (the 90th percentile) do happen, especially on higher ridges and drier benches around the county.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water to expect
sections.html:
Production here is generally solid for single-family homes. The median reported yield is 9.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells come in between 6.0 and 11.5 gpm. About 74% of tested wells fall in the 5–15 gpm band, which is more than enough for typical household use under Colorado’s exempt-well rules.

Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 14% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Those lower-yield wells can still work with storage and careful plumbing, but they’re less forgiving. On the high side, around 11% of wells test at 15+ gpm. Overall, Grand County’s fractured bedrock is variable hole-to-hole, but the odds favor a usable domestic well.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water level – how far down from the surface you first hit water – runs shallower than total depth. Countywide, the median static level is about 80 feet, with the middle half between 37 and 100 feet. That’s typical for mountain bedrock: you drill deeper than the water level to set casing and give the pump some submergence.

Looking at trends, median static level by decade deepened from about 35 feet in the 1970s to 60 feet in the 1980s and 90 feet in the 1990s, then improved to about 80 feet in the 2000s, 2010s, and 2020s. That suggests some early drawdown followed by a fairly stable plateau over the last few decades, not a steady ongoing decline.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling here and when
sections.html:
Grand County has a long well history, with permits on record back to the 1950s. Activity ramped up sharply in the 1970s and 1980s, with 1,422 and 1,382 permits in those decades. The 1990s and 2000s were the peak building years, at 2,618 and 2,337 permits. Even in the 2010s and 2020s there have been 970 and 908 new permits, and the newest record runs through 2026.

Most wells serve domestic or household use (about 86%), with smaller numbers for stock (3%), irrigation (1%), and monitoring (6%). The big drilling outfits in the records are Mcpherson Drilling Company with 1,840 wells, James Drilling with 720, and Virginia Drilling Co. Inc. with 447. All of this is in non–Denver Basin fractured rock, plus a small number of Alluvial and Troublesome aquifer wells.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost
sections.html:
Ground conditions here are fractured mountain bedrock – granite and gneiss – so pricing is per foot of hard-rock drilling. Typical drilling rates run around $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 190-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $12,400–$19,000.

Once you add pump, pressure tank, pitless adapter, trenching to the house, wire, and controls, a finished domestic well at that median depth typically comes out roughly $18,400–$31,000. Deeper wells toward the 300–500 foot range scale up from there. When you’re budgeting a land purchase, assume at least that median-cost window unless you have nearby well logs to justify aiming lower.

sections.heading: Key risks: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Even with good overall stats, there are a few real risks to weigh. Around 1% of wells come in under 1 gpm and 14% in the 1–5 gpm range, which can mean storage tanks and very conservative water use. Fractured-bedrock systems are also unpredictable – two wells a few hundred feet apart can behave very differently.

On the environmental side, within about 10 miles there are 10 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 85 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your well is unsafe, but it does mean water testing for metals and PFAS is smart. Plan your well and septic so they are well separated and downhill flow goes away from your water source.

sections.heading: Buying or building on land in Grand County
sections.html:
Before you close on land around places like Fraser, Winter Park, Granby, or Kremmling, pull neighboring well permits and pay close attention to depth and yield. With a county median depth of 190 feet and most wells between 100 and 325 feet, that’s your realistic planning band unless local logs tell a different story.

Most wells are domestic/household, so expect the usual Colorado exempt-well limits and rules. If you’re eyeing irrigation or multiple dwellings, talk to a water attorney or engineer about augmentation early. Budget in that $18,400–$31,000 range for a typical new well, and don’t skip a good water-quality panel, especially in areas with historic mining or mapped PFAS work.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Grand County, the median well depth is about 190 feet, but there’s a lot of variation. The middle half of wells fall between 100 and 325 feet. About 25% of wells are under 100 feet, while another 25% are between 300 and 600 feet, and about 7% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record in the county goes down 2,125 feet.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported yields in Grand County are generally strong for household use. The median pump yield is 9.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells produce between 6.0 and 11.5 gpm. Around 74% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range. Low-yield wells do occur: about 14% are in the 1–5 gpm band and 1% report under 1 gpm, which can require storage and careful management.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: Drilling here is mostly in hard fractured bedrock, at typical rates of about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 190-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone usually runs around $12,400–$19,000. A complete domestic well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is commonly in the $18,400–$31,000 range at that depth, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level data show an early deepening and then a leveling off. Median depth to water was about 35 feet in the 1970s, 60 feet in the 1980s, and 90 feet in the 1990s. Since the 2000s it has been around 80 feet in each decade (2000s, 2010s, 2020s). That pattern suggests some historical drawdown followed by a relatively stable water table over the last 20-plus years.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well and location. The county has 10 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 85 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so local geology and history matter. Many domestic wells are fine with basic treatment, but you should always test a new or existing well for bacteria, metals, and, in some areas, PFAS before relying on it for drinking water.
